## Overview

`QTLSim.jl` simulates the quantitative-genetic model of Pagel, Gardner and
Meade [@Pagel2025], who used it to ask how fast a population can track a steadily
changing environment before it goes extinct. Their simulations were run with QTSim, a C
program by Andrew Meade; this package is a Julia port of it, built around a fast
kernel that reproduces QTSim's output (see
[Validation against QTSim](../08_validation_against_qtsim/08_validation_against_qtsim.qmd)).
An optional categorical layer, loaded with Catlab, describes the population and its life
cycle as a composition of operators ([The categorical layer](../04_categorical_layer/04_categorical_layer.qmd)).

The model follows a population of $N$ diploid individuals with one quantitative trait.

- Each individual carries two copies of `NoQTL` loci. Its genotype $G$ is the sum of the
  allelic effects at all of them, and its phenotype is $z = G + E$, where the
  environmental deviation $E$ is drawn from $\mathcal{N}(0, V_E)$ at birth.
- Selection is on viability: an individual survives with probability
  $W(z) = \exp\!\left(-(z-\theta)^2 / 2\omega^2\right)$, a Gaussian fitness function
  with optimum $\theta$ and width $\omega$ (up to a constant close to one, which the
  package keeps exactly as QTSim computes it).
- The survivors mate at random. Each of the $N$ offspring has two distinct parents, each
  of which passes on a gamete made by recombining its two chromosomes.
- Each offspring chromosome receives a Poisson number of mutations, each adding a
  Gaussian effect to a randomly chosen locus.

This vignette runs the model once, looks at what it returns, and then lets the optimum
move, which is the experiment at the heart of the paper.

## Setup

```{julia}
using QTLSim
using CairoMakie, Printf, Statistics
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
```

## Parameters

A simulation is described by a `Params` value. Its defaults are QTSim's, and its fields follow
QTSim's options with a few differences in name: `Generations` is `NoGenerations`,
`RecombinationPoissonMean` is `RecombPoissonMean` and `OptimumMoveType` is `MoveType`,
and the two-value options `MoveFitnessSD` and `ChangeFitnessSD` are each split into a
generation and a value.
The phenotypic variance $V_P$ and heritability $h^2$ fix the genetic and environmental
variances the model aims for, $V_G = h^2 V_P$ and $V_E = (1-h^2) V_P$; the mutation
scalar $m$ sets the new variance mutation adds each generation, $V_m = m V_E$.

```{julia}
p = Params(PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 100, NoGenerations = 3000,
           PhenotypeVar = 0.02, Heritability = 0.4, MutationScalar = 0.004,
           MutationRatePerGamete = 1e-4, RecombPoissonMean = 3.0)

@printf("target genetic variance V_G = h²·V_P      %.4f\n", geneticVar(p))
@printf("environmental variance  V_E = (1−h²)·V_P  %.4f\n", envVar(p))
@printf("mutational input        V_m = m·V_E       %.2e per generation\n", muteVar(p))
@printf("fitness width           ω                 %.3f\n", initFitSD(p))
```

`MutationRatePerGamete` is the mutation rate per locus per gamete, so each chromosome
receives on average `NoQTL × MutationRatePerGamete` = 0.01 mutations per generation.
`RecombPoissonMean` is the mean number of crossover points drawn per gamete. When
`InitFitnessSD` is left at its default, the width $\omega$ is QTSim's "analytical"
value $\omega = V_G / \sqrt{m V_E}$; the next vignette explains where it comes from.

## A first run

`simulate` builds the population, runs it for `NoGenerations` generations and returns
one record per sampled generation (every generation here, since `Sample = 1`). The
genomes start at zero, so the genetic variance starts at zero too and builds up through
mutation.

```{julia}
out = simulate(p; seed = 1)
keys(out)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-first-run
#| fig-cap: "One population under stabilising selection. The mean phenotype stays near the optimum (zero), the genetic variance builds up from zero to a balance between mutation, selection and drift, and almost every individual survives selection each generation."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 300))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "mean phenotype")
lines!(ax1, out.gen, out.pheno_mean, color = :navy)
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "genetic variance")
lines!(ax2, out.gen, out.geno_var, color = :teal)
hlines!(ax2, [geneticVar(p)], color = :gray, linestyle = :dash)
ax3 = Axis(fig[1, 3], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "survivors")
lines!(ax3, out.gen, out.nsurv, color = :crimson)
fig
```

The dashed line is the target $h^2 V_P$. The variance the population actually maintains
is set by the balance of mutation, selection and drift, not by the target; the
[next vignette](../02_mutation_selection_balance/02_mutation_selection_balance.qmd)
compares it with theory.

```{julia}
late = out.gen .>= 2000
@printf("mean genetic variance over generations 2000–2999: %.4f\n", mean(out.geno_var[late]))
@printf("mean number of survivors:                          %.1f of %d\n",
        mean(out.nsurv[late]), p.PopSize)
```

## Reproducibility

Runs are driven by a seeded random-number generator, so the same seed gives the same
run, and a different seed gives a different realisation of the same process.

```{julia}
same = simulate(p; seed = 1)
other = simulate(p; seed = 2)
(same_seed_identical = same.geno_var == out.geno_var,
 other_seed_identical = other.geno_var == out.geno_var)
```

## Letting the optimum move

In the paper's experiments the optimum stands still while the population reaches
equilibrium, then moves by a fixed amount $d$ every generation
(`MoveType = :continuous`, starting at `MoveFitnessSDGen`). A population that can keep
up follows the optimum with a constant lag; one that cannot falls further and further
behind, its survival collapses, and it goes extinct. Here the same population faces a
slow and a fast rate of change, starting at generation 2000. Rates are easiest to
compare in units of the phenotypic standard deviation, which we measure just before the
move.

```{julia}
moving(d) = Params(p; NoGenerations = 3000, MoveFitnessSDGen = 2000,
                   MoveFitnessSD = d, MoveType = :continuous)
slow = simulate(moving(0.002); seed = 1)
fast = simulate(moving(0.05); seed = 1)
sdP = sqrt(mean(slow.pheno_var[1900 .<= slow.gen .< 2000]))
@printf("phenotypic SD before the move: %.3f\n", sdP)
@printf("slow: d = 0.002 is %4.1f%% of an SD per generation; extinct: %s\n",
        100 * 0.002 / sdP, slow.extinct)
@printf("fast: d = 0.05  is %4.1f%% of an SD per generation; extinct at generation %d\n",
        100 * 0.05 / sdP, fast.extinct_gen)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-moving
#| fig-cap: "The optimum (dashed) starts moving at generation 2000. At the slow rate the mean phenotype (solid) keeps pace and survival stays high; at the fast rate the population falls further and further behind, survival collapses and the population dies out."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 330))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "phenotype / optimum",
           limits = ((1800, 3000), nothing))
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "survivors",
           limits = ((1800, 3000), (0, 1050)))
for (r, c, name) in ((slow, :teal, "d = 0.002"), (fast, :crimson, "d = 0.05"))
    lines!(ax1, r.gen, r.pheno_mean, color = c, label = name)
    lines!(ax1, r.gen, r.theta, color = c, linestyle = :dash)
    lines!(ax2, r.gen, r.nsurv, color = c, label = name)
end
axislegend(ax1, position = :lt)
fig
```

The slow rate, about 1% of a phenotypic standard deviation per generation, is well within
what this population can track: it holds a lot of genetic variance, and its narrow
fitness function turns a small lag into strong selection. At a quarter of a standard
deviation per generation it dies within two hundred generations. Across
the range of populations the paper simulated, sustainable change is limited to a few per
cent of a standard deviation per generation;
[Adaptation to a moving optimum](../03_moving_optimum/03_moving_optimum.qmd) measures
this the way the paper does, and
[Replicating Pagel, Gardner and Meade (2025)](../09_replicating_pagel_2025/09_replicating_pagel_2025.qmd)
reproduces the paper's results.
